title: No prosecution for SIR-dropped voters who reapply, Election Commission tells Supreme Court
dek: In an affidavit, the Commission put on record that voters left off draft rolls can file Form 6 without risk of a false-declaration case, and accepted that errors may have crept in while removing dead and absent voters.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Election Commission of India has told the Supreme Court that voters whose names were left off the draft rolls during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) will not be prosecuted for reapplying on Form 6, the application normally used to enrol new voters. In an affidavit filed on Saturday, the Commission also accepted that errors may have occurred in removing names of dead and non-existent voters during the exercise, according to reports.

The Commission said no prosecution would be initiated "merely on the ground that the applicant/elector was previously enrolled in the electoral roll(s) prior to the SIR", provided the applicant is not already registered in another assembly or parliamentary constituency and the declaration is otherwise lawful, the reports said. The affidavit was filed in petitions alleging large-scale deletions from the rolls in Maharashtra and Delhi.

## Why it matters

Form 6 requires applicants to declare that they are applying to be enrolled for the first time. Some voters who had been on earlier rolls feared that signing that declaration could be treated as false and expose them to prosecution under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, which punishes false declarations. The Commission had already told state chief electoral officers on 3 November that such applicants should not face Section 31 action; the affidavit puts that position on the court's record.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana had said at an earlier hearing that no one would be prosecuted for filing Form 6 to get back on the rolls, according to reports.

## What the Commission set out

The affidavit, as reported, says:

- Voters left out of draft rolls under the "ASDD" category (absent, shifted, dead or duplicate) can submit a fresh enumeration form to the electoral registration officer or assistant officer for their current address, or online with an e-signature on the Commission's ECINET platform.
- Voters who have moved can submit the form with proof of address, or use a "book a call with BLO" option to have a booth-level officer visit; their forms will be processed under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and they will keep their existing voter ID (EPIC) number.
- Voters who already filed Form 6 during the SIR need not file again.
- Chief electoral officers must publicise the clarification, including in local languages.

The Commission said it had taken note of the court's suggestion that it contact voters excluded under the ASDD category and help them get back on the rolls where eligible. It again rejected claims that Form 6 itself had been amended, the reports said.

## The political fight

Opposition parties, including the Congress, the Trinamool Congress, the DMK and the Left, have accused the Commission of using the SIR to strike genuine voters off the rolls in several states, and have challenged the exercise in the Supreme Court. The Commission says the revision is authorised by the Constitution and the 1950 Act and is needed to clean the rolls of dead, shifted and duplicate entries, and that no name is removed without due process. The scale of deletions in West Bengal, put at about 58 lakh in a petition by a Trinamool MP, has been one of the sharpest points of dispute.

## What happens next

The Supreme Court is due to take up a batch of petitions on the SIR and the functioning of the Commission on Tuesday, 17 November, according to reports. In Uttar Pradesh, the draft roll for the 2027 Assembly election is due to be published the same day.
